content.text:
’ rebuttal says “the Legislature’s nearly unanimous vote to place Prop. 43 on the ballot” shows courts “exceeded voters’ intent.” It was signed by Jon Coupal (Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association), Michael Hedges (California Small Business Association) and Greg Van Dyke (California Consumer Advocates for Affordability and Safety) (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, head of Reform California, told the Sacramento Bee editorial board he could find savings “to eliminate the need for a tax increase on any ballot in the state of California this cycle” (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/confused-about-how-to-vote-on-proposition-43-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2csuRb)).
Evolve California argues the measure would make California the hardest state in the country to raise local revenue, the Sacramento Bee reported (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/should-local-taxes-require-two-thirds-voter-approval-proposition-43-explained/ar-AA2crlnQ)).
California YIMBY says the measure would make it harder to raise money for “infrastructure upgrades, affordable housing trust funds, and public transportation,” and would push cities toward higher impact fees on new housing (California YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-43-2026/)).
Mott Smith of the Council of Infill Builders, who backed ULA changes, said the industry donors behind the Jarvis initiative “really got absolutely nothing” from the deal (LAist (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure)).
Checking the main claims against official records.
Claim Who makes it What official records show
Restores the two-thirds vote for local special taxes Yes campaign (argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)) The text requires two-thirds for new, increased or extended special taxes, including those proposed by initiative, from Jan. 1, 2027 (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). Taxes already approved are not affected (official summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/title-summary.htm)).
Guarantees voters the right to vote on all local taxes Yes campaign The Constitution already requires voter approval of local general taxes (majority) and special taxes (two-thirds) (Art. XIII C, Sec. 2 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C)). Proposition 43 adds no new election requirement for general taxes (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
Requires governments to spend tax money on the purpose voters approved Yes campaign The text contains no spending rule. It sets vote thresholds and the property-tax limit only (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
Protects homeowners from real estate transfer taxes up to 6% Yes campaign The text does not mention transfer taxes. It would require two-thirds for a new or higher transfer tax only if it is a special tax proposed by voters (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). LA’s ULA rates are 4% and 5.5% (County election results (https://results.lavote.gov/text-results/4300)).
2,000 new or higher local taxes in the past decade Yes campaign We did not find an official count to check this against.
One-third of voters (33.4%) could block a tax No campaign A two-thirds rule means a measure with 66.6% yes fails. The Budget Center gives the example of 35% blocking 65% (California Budget & Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/)).
The Legislature voted nearly unanimously Yes campaign Senate 35-1 and Assembly 68-2, with 13 members not voting. The author and legislative leaders reached the deal to remove another measure (ACA 22 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22); LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits)).
Makes it harder to fund fire and police No campaign It applies to special taxes proposed by voters. Council-placed special taxes already need two-thirds, and general taxes that can pay for police and fire still need a majority (Art. XIII C, Sec. 2 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C)). The Legislative Analyst says local revenue “could be lower in the future” (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)).
Who supports and opposes it
Supporters
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association of California, California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, California Small Business Association and California Consumer Advocates for Affordability and Safety, which signed the guide arguments (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
California Business Roundtable, through its Issues PAC, the largest donor (Cal-Access, committee 1484860 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484860)).
California Republican Party (CAGOP endorsements (https://cagop.org/endorsements/)).
Reform California and Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (California Budget & Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/); Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/should-local-taxes-require-two-thirds-voter-approval-proposition-43-explained/ar-AA2crlnQ)).
State Senators Shannon Grove, Tony Strickland and Suzette Valladares, whose ballot measure committees paid for slate mailers supporting it (Cal-Access raw data (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
Opponents
California Professional Firefighters, Nurse Alliance of SEIU California, California School Employees Association, California Federation of Teachers, Californians Against Waste, Communities for a Better Environment, AAPI Force, Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California and Sierra Business Council, as listed in the argument against (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
California Democratic Party (Inland Valley News (https://inlandvalleynews.com/california-democratic-party-endorses-2026-general-election-candidates-ballot-measures/); KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-43)).
California State Association of Counties and SEIU California (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-43)).
Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, the author (LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits)), and Evolve California (California Budget & Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/)).
California YIMBY (California YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-43-2026/)).
The League of California Cities’ CITIPAC gave $250,000.01 to the No committee (Cal-Access, committee 1492508 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1492508)). A contribution is not the same as a formal endorsement.
Editorial boards.
Yes: the Southern California News Group, in the Daily News and Orange County Register (Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/08/09/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-43-to-make-it-harder-to-raise-taxes/); Orange County Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/09/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-43-to-make-it-harder-to-raise-taxes/)), and the San Diego Union-Tribune (San Diego Union-Tribune (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/04/vote-yes-on-prop-43-to-block-state-supreme-courts-rewrite-of-tax-laws/)). The Mercury News and East Bay Times editorial boards also recommend yes, writing that it “merits support” (Mercury News, Oct. 17, 2026 (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/17/endorsement-back-prop-43-restore-voter-approved-restrictions-on-local-taxes-proposition-13/)).
No: the Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/confused-about-how-to-vote-on-proposition-43-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2csuRb)).
Neither: the San Francisco Chronicle editorial board wrote, “We don’t support Prop 43 because it further cements a broken system. But ultimately, we won’t oppose it, either” (San Francisco Chronicle, Oct. 23, 2026 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-43-ballot-california-22477053.php)).
We found no LA Times editorial board position as of Sept. 30, 2026.
Money for and against
For Proposition 43 Against Proposition 43
Committees Two: Yes on Prop 43 - The Local Taxpayer Protection Act (ID 1484860) and Yes on Prop. 43, a Project of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (ID 1493012) One: No on Prop 43: Stop the Local Taxpayer Deception Act, sponsored by labor organizations (ID 1492508)
Raised, Jan. 1, 2025 to Oct. 17, 2026 $15,417,784.02 $7,742,284.74
Spent, same period $15,567,031.80 $6,622,177.15
Cash on hand, Oct. 17, 2026 $244,784.93 $1,152,357.59
Late contributions reported Oct. 18 to Nov. 1 $2,141,383.93 $1,459,000
Source: the committees’ campaign statements for committee 1484860 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484860), committee 1493012 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1493012) and committee 1492508 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1492508), read from the Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip) dated Nov. 2, 2026, and added up by CityHallPass. The latest statements cover Sept. 20 to Oct. 17 (1484860 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3215138&amendid=0); 1493012 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3214623&amendid=0); 1492508 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3215820&amendid=0)). Late contributions are from the committees’ 24-hour reports filed Oct. 19 to Nov. 1, including (1484860: Oct. 19 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3212581&amendid=0), Oct. 20 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3213212&amendid=0), Oct. 21 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3214087&amendid=0), Oct. 22 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3215517&amendid=0), Oct. 22 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3215661&amendid=0); 1493012: Oct. 20 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3213215&amendid=0), Oct. 21 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3213987&amendid=0); 1492508: Oct. 20 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3213523&amendid=0)). The No committee reported $32,250 in unpaid bills on Oct. 17. The Secretary of State’s compiled totals (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-43-aca-22-wicks-local-taxes-limitation-res-ch-132-2026) still ran only through Aug. 2 when checked on Sept. 30.
Most of the Yes money was raised before the June 25 deal, when the main committee was working to qualify the Jarvis initiative. Of the $16.68 million in contributions to committee 1484860 through Nov. 1, $2,531,896.67 came in on or after June 25 (Cal-Access, committee 1484860 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484860)). It paid National Political Consultants $12,808,893.92 for petition circulation, 96.5% of its payments. It had $384,461.54 in unpaid bills on Oct. 17 (Cal-Access raw data (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
Who is giving
Method: every itemized contribution on the committees’ Form 460 statements from Jan. 1, 2025 to Oct. 17, 2026, plus late contribution reports through Nov. 1, from the Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip). Categories are ours, based on the donor’s name and reported employer.
For: the main Yes committee (ID 1484860).
75 donors gave $16,682,288.53. The California Business Roundtable Issues PAC gave $11,640,000 (69.8%) in 21 payments from Nov. 26, 2025 to Oct. 29, 2026.
Protect Prop. 13, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association’s general committee, gave $1,038,217.78 in mailers and phone calls from January to March 2026. Right Path California Issues PAC gave $584,310.54 in October, $168,724.25 of it in kind.
Real estate owners, developers, managers and brokers gave $2,486,436.13 (14.9%), led by Douglas Emmett Properties ($1,000,000), Kilroy Realty ($1,000,000), McCourt Partners Real Estate ($100,000), Andrew Schwartzberg of Housing Inc. ($100,000) and Moss Management Services ($85,000). That is 62.1% of the money that did not come from the Roundtable or the Jarvis committee.
Other large donors: 1800 Capital, Inc. ($500,000) and Jerry Greenberg, CEO of Sushi Nozawa ($250,000).
98.9% of the money came from donors with California addresses.
Type of donor Donors Amount Share
California Business Roundtable Issues PAC 1 $11,640,000.00 69.8%
Real estate firms and people 41 $2,486,436.13 14.9%
Other businesses, groups and individuals 32 $1,517,634.62 9.1%
Howard Jarvis committee (in-kind) 1 $1,038,217.78 6.2%
Source: Cal-Access, committee 1484860 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484860), analyzed by CityHallPass. Related entities of one owner are counted separately.
For: the Howard Jarvis Yes committee (ID 1493012). It raised $850,780.55 through Oct. 17. Of that, $475,000 came from Protect Prop. 13, and $580,951.89 was itemized from about 730 donors, most giving $500 or less. It spent $458,804 on radio through Drew Hayes Media and paid $48,490.05 to the association’s spokesperson for campaign work (Cal-Access, committee 1493012 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1493012)).
Against (ID 1492508). 36 donors gave $9,201,284.74 through Oct. 30, all from July 30 on. Unions gave $6,776,747.93 (73.7%). SEIU committees gave $3,598,928.03 (39.1%): the SEIU California State Council ($1,503,928.03), SEIU Local 2015 ($1,000,000), SEIU Local 1021 ($500,000), SEIU Local 721 ($500,000), SEIU Local 99 ($75,000), SEIU Local 121RN ($10,000) and SEIU’s national fund ($10,000). Other donors: California Professional Firefighters ($846,379), the Western States and North Coast regional councils of Carpenters ($500,000 each), the California Teachers Association ($500,000), California Federation of Teachers ($250,000), Operating Engineers Local 3 ($250,000), AFSCME committees ($275,000), the California Alliance for Jobs ($500,000), the Southern California Partnership for Jobs ($500,000), the League of California Cities CITIPAC ($250,000.01), the NPH Action Fund ($202,805.15), the San Francisco Foundation ($300,000), the California Community Foundation ($200,000), the Silicon Valley Community Foundation ($100,000), the ACLU of Northern California ($100,000) and Million More Voters, sponsored by the California Labor Federation ($50,000) (Cal-Access, committee 1492508 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1492508)). The California Community Foundation, which listed a Los Angeles address, also gave $400,000 to the City’s Measure FD campaign (our Measure FD page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/measure-fd)).
Where committee donors get their money. From the committees’ own state filings in the Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip):
California Business Roundtable Issues PAC (Cal-Access (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1264590)): $14,105,651 in itemized receipts on statements covering Oct. 20, 2024 to Oct. 17, 2026, led by Peter Thiel ($3,000,000), Eric Schmidt ($2,580,301), Kim DeGeorge ($1,930,000), Farmers Group ($1,500,000), Brookfield Property Group ($1,000,000) and Chris Larsen ($750,000). The PAC’s receipts are not earmarked, so these donors did not necessarily pay for Proposition 43.
SEIU California State Council for Working People (Cal-Access (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=960895)): its itemized receipts from Oct. 20, 2024 to Oct. 17, 2026 were $100,385.08, all from the SEIU California State Council itself.
SEIU Local 1021 Issues PAC (Cal-Access (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1296947)): all itemized receipts came from SEIU Local 1021.
League of California Cities CITIPAC (Cal-Access (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1254399)): $547,429.41 in itemized receipts from Oct. 20, 2024 to Oct. 17, 2026, 33.3% from the League itself and the rest from businesses such as waste haulers and utilities.
California Professional Firefighters Ballot Issues Committee (Cal-Access (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=861767)): its only itemized receipt on these statements was $250,000 from the IAFF’s FirePAC.
Outside spending
Committees reported these independent expenditures naming Proposition 43 on Form 496 through Oct. 25 (Cal-Access raw data (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)):
Supporting: Reform California with Carl DeMaio, ballot measure committee, $148,862.20 (door hangers, lawn signs, slate mailers, campaign management); Senator Tony Strickland’s committee, $14,000; Senator Shannon Grove’s committee, $10,500; Senator Suzette Valladares’s committee, $3,000 (the three senators’ committees for slate mailers and voter guides); Republican Party of San Diego County, $2,531.67 (literature).
Opposing: Faith Votes, sponsored by PICO California Action Fund, $38,720.83 (digital ads, phone banking); ACLU California Action Issues Committee, $8,988.70 (voter guide, digital ads); Million Voter Project Action Fund, $5,299.09; ACLU Foundation of San Diego & Imperial Counties, $5,206.21; Justice CA: Isaac Bryan Ballot Measure Committee, $5,000 (slate mailer); Community Partners, $3,915.14; Youth Power PAC, $3,815.66; Council of Community Housing Organizations, $3,120.71; AAPI Equity Alliance, $986.55. Many of these amounts are the filers’ estimates.
Independent analysis
Legislative Analyst. Local tax revenue “could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be.” The effect “is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters” (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)).
California Budget & Policy Center (a nonprofit that takes no position on measures). It says the rule would reach all special taxes proposed by voters for cities, counties, special districts and school districts, because all taxes of special districts and school districts count as special taxes. It lists ULA among recent majority-approved initiative taxes, with 58% (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/)).
Burke, Williams & Sorensen. The measure “applies prospectively only,” so “local ballot measures approved on or before the November 2026 election are no longer at risk of being invalidated” (California City News (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html)).

Claim Who makes it What official records show

2,000 new or higher local taxes in the past decade Yes campaign We did not find an official count to check this against.

’ rebuttal says “the Legislature’s nearly unanimous vote to place Prop. 43 on the ballot” shows courts “exceeded voters’ intent.” It was signed by Jon Coupal (Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association), Michael Hedges (California Small Business Association) and Greg Van Dyke (California Consumer Advocates for Affordability and Safety) (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, head of Reform California, told the Sacramento Bee editorial board he could find savings “to eliminate the need for a tax increase on any ballot in the state of California this cycle” (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/confused-about-how-to-vote-on-proposition-43-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2csuRb)).
Evolve California argues the measure would make California the hardest state in the country to raise local revenue, the Sacramento Bee reported (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/should-local-taxes-require-two-thirds-voter-approval-proposition-43-explained/ar-AA2crlnQ)).
California YIMBY says the measure would make it harder to raise money for “infrastructure upgrades, affordable housing trust funds, and public transportation,” and would push cities toward higher impact fees on new housing (California YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-43-2026/)).
Mott Smith of the Council of Infill Builders, who backed ULA changes, said the industry donors behind the Jarvis initiative “really got absolutely nothing” from the deal (LAist (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure)).
Checking the main claims against official records.
Claim Who makes it What official records show
Restores the two-thirds vote for local special taxes Yes campaign (argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)) The text requires two-thirds for new, increased or extended special taxes, including those proposed by initiative, from Jan. 1, 2027 (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). Taxes already approved are not affected (official summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/title-summary.htm)).
Guarantees voters the right to vote on all local taxes Yes campaign The Constitution already requires voter approval of local general taxes (majority) and special taxes (two-thirds) (Art. XIII C, Sec. 2 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C)). Proposition 43 adds no new election requirement for general taxes (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
Requires governments to spend tax money on the purpose voters approved Yes campaign The text contains no spending rule. It sets vote thresholds and the property-tax limit only (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
Protects homeowners from real estate transfer taxes up to 6% Yes campaign The text does not mention transfer taxes. It would require two-thirds for a new or higher transfer tax only if it is a special tax proposed by voters (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). LA’s ULA rates are 4% and 5.5% (County election results (https://results.lavote.gov/text-results/4300)).
2,000 new or higher local taxes in the past decade Yes campaign We did not find an official count to check this against.
One-third of voters (33.4%) could block a tax No campaign A two-thirds rule means a measure with 66.6% yes fails. The Budget Center gives the example of 35% blocking 65% (California Budget & Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/)).
The Legislature voted nearly unanimously Yes campaign Senate 35-1 and Assembly 68-2, with 13 members not voting. The author and legislative leaders reached the deal to remove another measure (ACA 22 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22); LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits)).
Makes it harder to fund fire and police No campaign It applies to special taxes proposed by voters. Council-placed special taxes already need two-thirds, and general taxes that can pay for police and fire still need a majority (Art. XIII C, Sec. 2 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C)). The Legislative Analyst says local revenue “could be lower in the future” (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)).
Who supports and opposes it
Supporters
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association of California, California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, California Small Business Association and California Consumer Advocates for Affordability and Safety, which signed the guide arguments (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
California Business Roundtable, through its Issues PAC, the largest donor (Cal-Access, committee 1484860 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484860)).
California Republican Party (CAGOP endorsements (https://cagop.org/endorsements/)).
Reform California and Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (California Budget & Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/); Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/should-local-taxes-require-two-thirds-voter-approval-proposition-43-explained/ar-AA2crlnQ)).
State Senators Shannon Grove, Tony Strickland and Suzette Valladares, whose ballot measure committees paid for slate mailers supporting it (Cal-Access raw data (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
Opponents
California Professional Firefighters, Nurse Alliance of SEIU California, California School Employees Association, California Federation of Teachers, Californians Against Waste, Communities for a Better Environment, AAPI Force, Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California and Sierra Business Council, as listed in the argument against (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
California Democratic Party (Inland Valley News (https://inlandvalleynews.com/california-democratic-party-endorses-2026-general-election-candidates-ballot-measures/); KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-43)).
California State Association of Counties and SEIU California (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-43)).
Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, the author (LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits)), and Evolve California (California Budget & Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/)).
California YIMBY (California YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-43-2026/)).
The League of California Cities’ CITIPAC gave $250,000.01 to the No committee (Cal-Access, committee 1492508 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1492508)). A contribution is not the same as a formal endorsement.
Editorial boards.
Yes: the Southern California News Group, in the Daily News and Orange County Register (Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/08/09/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-43-to-make-it-harder-to-raise-taxes/); Orange County Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/09/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-43-to-make-it-harder-to-raise-taxes/)), and the San Diego Union-Tribune (San Diego Union-Tribune (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/04/vote-yes-on-prop-43-to-block-state-supreme-courts-rewrite-of-tax-laws/)). The Mercury News and East Bay Times editorial boards also recommend yes, writing that it “merits support” (Mercury News, Oct. 17, 2026 (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/17/endorsement-back-prop-43-restore-voter-approved-restrictions-on-local-taxes-proposition-13/)).
No: the Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/confused-about-how-to-vote-on-proposition-43-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2csuRb)).
Neither: the San Francisco Chronicle editorial board wrote, “We don’t support Prop 43 because it further cements a broken system. But ultimately, we won’t oppose it, either” (San Francisco Chronicle, Oct. 23, 2026 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-43-ballot-california-22477053.php)).

- The measure was placed on the ballot by Democratic lawmakers as part of a deal to remove the broader HJTA initiative; its own author opposes it. Governor Newsom — let me check his position. He brokered the deal but I haven't seen his endorsement. The Democratic Party opposes it.

**Electoral context 2026:** Midterm election in California. The electorate in a midterm tends to be more Democratic/liberal, which favors the No side. Also, Prop 40 (billionaires tax) is on the ballot; the Democratic governor candidates etc.

Given all polls show No leading by 9-13 points just days before the election, with roughly 8-19% undecided, the No side is clearly more likely to win. **TAX TURMOIL:** California relies on local taxes to maintain roads and bridges, and keep its vast transit system from crumbling.
A proposition on the November ballot would make passing and renewing those taxes much, much harder.
Proposition 43, backed by anti-tax advocates like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, would change the state’s current system so that two-thirds of voters must approve issue-specific taxes placed on the ballot through citizens’ initiatives for those proposals to pass.

Based on my extensive research, I have a clear picture:

**Proposition 43 (Nov. 3, 2026, California)** would raise the vote threshold for citizen-initiated local special taxes from a simple majority to two-thirds. - **Polling — every public poll shows the "No" side leading:**
  - PPIC final poll (Oct 16–22): **42% Yes / 55% No** (only 3% undecided; No's lead grew from 51% in September)
  - Berkeley IGS (Oct 19–25): **36% Yes / 46% No** (up from 31–40 in September)
  - Support is below 50% in every region, with only 28% of Democrats in favor — fatal in a deep-blue midterm electorate (Becerra leads the governor's race 61–37 in the same poll)

- **Opposition coalition:** Governor Newsom (announced opposition Oct. 12), the California Democratic Party, League of California Cities, County associations, 50+ mayors, 100+ local governments, firefighters/teachers/nurses/SEIU unions, and even the measure's own author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, who publicly campaigns against it

- **Support:** mainly HJTA, CalTax, and the Republican Party — a distinct minority coalition in California

- **Funding:** The Yes side's headline $16–17M is mostly pre-deal signature-gathering money; the No side has $9M+ of active union money and a decisive polling trend in its favor

The "Yes" side (Prop 43 passing) trails by 9–13 points in the final polls with virtually no undecided voters left, against a unified Democratic/local-government opposition in a Democratic-leaning midterm electorate.

43
LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO RAISE REVENUES FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT SERVICES. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes. Supporters: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce Opponents: California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 43 protects taxpayers by restoring Proposition 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes, including sales taxes, real estate taxes and utility taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters. Vote yes.
CON
PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES including fire protection, 911 response, schools, roads, hospitals and affordable housing. It doesn’t cut your taxes and lets just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want. Protect your vote and majority rule. Vote NO on Proposition 43.

# 2026 California Proposition 43
**Proposition 43** is a proposed legislative constitutional amendment on the November 3, 2026, ballot in California.
Starting on January 1, 2027, Proposition 43 would restore the two-thirds voter approval requirement to impose, extend, or increase a local special (legally dedicated) tax under Proposition 13 for any proposed special tax that qualifies for the ballot under the local initiative power.^[1]^ Proposition 43 would also prohibit local governments, including under the local initiative power, from imposing additional ad valorem taxes on real property (taxes based on the assessed value of property), except as otherwise allowed under the California Constitution.^[2]^
Proposition 43 was proposed to overturn appellate court rulings following the 2017 *Upland* decision by the California Supreme Court,^[3]^ which created a distinction between taxes proposed by the governing body of a local government and taxes proposed under the local initiative power for purposes of applying the two-thirds voter approval requirement for special taxes under Proposition 13.

Proposition 43 : Two-thirds vote for voter-proposed local special taxes
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 43 would require a two-thirds vote to approve local special taxes that voters put on the ballot by petition, starting January 1, 2027. Special taxes are taxes dedicated to a specific purpose. Special taxes placed on the ballot by a city council or other local board already need two-thirds, but court decisions let voter-proposed special taxes pass with a simple majority. It would also bar local governments and voters from adopting new taxes based on property value, with exceptions already in the Constitution.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 43
Vote needed for a local special tax proposed by voter petition Majority today; two-thirds for measures approved after Jan. 1, 2027, if it passes
Effect on City Measure FD (same ballot) None under the official summary: FD needs a majority
How it got here Legislative deal on June 25, 2026 that removed a broader Howard Jarvis initiative. Senate 35-1, Assembly 68-2
Money raised, Jan. 2025 to Nov. 1, 2026 For: $17.56 million (two committees). Against: $9.20 million
Largest donor For: California Business Roundtable Issues PAC, $11.64 million. Against: SEIU California State Council, $1.5 million
Latest public polls PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 42% yes, 55% no. Berkeley IGS, Oct. 19-25: 36% yes, 46% no
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures come from the committees' state campaign statements and late contribution reports (Cal-Access).
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , The details , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 43 mean?
Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
What does a no vote on Proposition 43 mean?
Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
What would Proposition 43 cost?
The Legislative Analyst says local governments' tax revenue could be lower in the future than it otherwise would be, because certain taxes would be harder to pass. The actual effect is unknown and depends on future decisions by local governments and voters. The analysis gives no dollar figure.
What it means for the City of LA
Future citizen-initiative special taxes in the City of Los Angeles, such as a sales tax for one department or a transfer tax like Measure ULA, would need two-thirds of the vote instead of a majority, starting January 1, 2027. The official summary says it applies to measures approved after that date, so the City's Measure FD on this ballot is decided by majority vote. Taxes the City Council puts on the ballot are not changed: general taxes still need a majority and special taxes already need two-thirds. The Legislative Analyst does not estimate the effect on the City.
The details
Official title Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Legislative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by the Legislature (ACA 22)
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide
The question on your ballot
Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes. Supporters: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce Opponents: California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA.
What would change
Today If Proposition 43 passes
Local special tax placed on the ballot by a city council, county board or district Two-thirds of voters must approve (State Constitution, Art. XIII C, Sec. 2(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C)) No change (text of Proposition 43 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Local special tax placed on the ballot by voter petition A majority can approve it, under recent court decisions (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)) Two-thirds of voters must approve any new, increased or extended special tax proposed by voters, beginning Jan. 1, 2027 (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm))
Local general tax (money can go to any purpose) A majority of voters must approve (State Constitution, Art. XIII C, Sec. 2(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C)) No change. The text covers only special taxes and property taxes (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
New local taxes based on property value Limited by Proposition 13 and later amendments No local government, “including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power,” may impose “ad valorem taxes on real property,” except as Article XIII D, Section 3(a)(1) already allows (text, Sec. 4.5(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Taxes voters approved before 2027 In effect Not affected. The Attorney General’s summary says the measure “Applies to voter-proposed ballot measures approved after January 1, 2027” (official title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/title-summary.htm))
Proposition 43 adds one section, Section 4.5, to Article XIII A of the State Constitution, the article created by Proposition 13 in 1978 (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). “Local government” and “special tax” keep their existing constitutional meanings. The Legislative Analyst’s analysis does not discuss the property-tax part, subdivision (b) (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)). The Sacramento Bee described it as generally barring new taxes based on property values, “with exceptions for certain voter-approved taxes used to repay bonds” (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/should-local-taxes-require-two-thirds-voter-approval-proposition-43-explained/ar-AA2crlnQ)).
What it means for the City of Los Angeles
Measure FD on this ballot. The City’s Initiative Ordinance FD, a half-cent sales tax for the Fire Department, is a special tax placed on the Nov. 3 ballot by voter petition. The City’s impartial summary says FD takes effect if a majority approves it (City pamphlet (https://cityclerk.lacity.org/election/ENG201_NOV-2026_Voter_Info_Pamphlet.pdf#page=91)). Proposition 43 “Applies to voter-proposed ballot measures approved after January 1, 2027,” the Attorney General’s summary says (official title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/title-summary.htm)). Elena Q. Gerli of the law firm Burke, Williams & Sorensen wrote that “local tax measures on the November 2026 ballot are still governed by the current majority-vote rule” (California City News (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html)). The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association’s argument against FD says FD “would squeeze through the loophole” before Proposition 43 takes effect in January 2027 (City pamphlet, argument against FD (https://cityclerk.lacity.org/election/ENG201_NOV-2026_Voter_Info_Pamphlet.pdf#page=97)). We found no official analysis that says otherwise. See our Measure FD page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/measure-fd).
Measure ULA. City voters approved Measure ULA, a citizen initiative that taxes property sales over $5 million at 4% and sales of $10 million or more at 5.5%, with 57.77% of the vote in November 2022 (County election results (https://results.lavote.gov/text-results/4300)). That share is below two-thirds. Proposition 43 does not undo taxes already approved (Burke, Williams & Sorensen (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html)). The Howard Jarvis initiative that Proposition 43 replaced would have eliminated ULA and similar taxes, LAist reported (LAist, June 26, 2026 (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure)). ULA has raised $1.2 billion since April 2023, LAist reported (LAist (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure)). The Legislative Analyst says that, beginning Jan. 1, 2027, “any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote” (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)). The City’s Proposition TE on this ballot, placed by the Council, would exempt some Palisades Fire victims from ULA (our Proposition TE page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/measure-te)).
Future City petitions. The City Clerk’s petition list shows citizen tax initiatives cleared to circulate into late 2027, including two gross receipts taxes tied to the ratio of executive to worker pay (petitions expiring Nov. 12 and Dec. 8, 2027). A half-cent sales tax for Recreation and Parks received a title in December 2025 but is not shown as approved for circulation (City Clerk petition status (https://clerk.lacity.gov/elections/petition-and-measure-info/petition-status)). The list does not say whether each tax would be general or special. Only special taxes would face the new two-thirds rule (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
Council-placed taxes. Proposition 43 does not change the vote needed for taxes the City Council places on the ballot. General taxes still need a majority and special taxes still need two-thirds (State Constitution, Art. XIII C, Sec. 2 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C); Aleshire & Wynder (https://www.awattorneys.com/client-updates/proposition-43-aca-22-could-reshape-local-tax-initiatives-what-california-cities-should-know-before-2027/)).
We found no official position on Proposition 43 from the Mayor, the City Council or the LA County Board of Supervisors as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
Proposition 43 began as Assembly Constitutional Amendment 22 by Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (D-Oakland). The resolution says it was proposed with “two-thirds of the membership of each house concurring” (text as quoted by Burke, Williams & Sorensen (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html)).
2017: In California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland , the State Supreme Court ruled that a tax measure placed on the ballot by citizen initiative needs only a majority, according to Burke, Williams & Sorensen (California City News (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html)). The Legislative Analyst says “recent court decisions” allow majority approval of voter-proposed special taxes (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)).
Nov. 8, 2022: City of LA voters approved Measure ULA with 57.77% (County election results (https://results.lavote.gov/text-results/4300)).
Late 2025 to early 2026: The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association collected signatures for Initiative 1983, the “Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13.” Burke says it would have raised the vote for voter-initiated tax measures to two-thirds, capped local real estate transfer taxes at the state base rate, and voided noncompliant property-related taxes by the end of 2028 (California City News (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html)). Its committee, then named “Californians to Restore Local Taxpayers’ Right to Vote on Taxes,” paid National Political Consultants $12.8 million for petition circulation (Cal-Access, committee 1484860 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484860)). Real estate developers and investors paid for the initiative, LAist reported (LAist (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure)).
ACA 13: The Legislature had placed ACA 13 (Ward) on the ballot. It would have required a measure that raises a vote threshold to pass by that same higher threshold, which Burke says would have meant the Jarvis initiative needed two-thirds (California City News (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html)).
June 25, 2026: Just before the deadline to remove measures from the ballot, the initiative’s proponents, Governor Gavin Newsom and legislative leaders announced a deal. Initiative 1983 and ACA 13 were withdrawn and replaced by ACA 22. The Secretary of State records that ACA 13 was removed from the ballot that day under ACA 21, Resolution Chapter 131 (Secretary of State, qualified measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/qualified-ballot-measures); Burke, Williams & Sorensen (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html); LAist (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure)). ACA 22 was introduced and passed that day: 68-2 in the Assembly and 35-1 in the Senate. Assemblymembers Alex Lee and Nick Schultz and Senator Scott Wiener voted no. It was filed with the Secretary of State as Resolution Chapter 132 at 4:40 p.m. (ACA 22 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22); ACA 22 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22)).
July 1, 2026: The City Council voted 14-0 to shelve a City measure that would have exempted new apartment buildings from ULA for 10 years, and 13-1 to place a Palisades Fire exemption on the ballot, now Proposition TE (LAist, July 1, 2026 (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-council-mansion-tax-measure-ula-november-ballot-measure-2026-vote)).
Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, called the deal “a tremendous turnaround” (LAist (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure)). Wicks said getting the Jarvis measure off the ballot protected local revenue from ULA and other transfer taxes (LAist (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure)). She now opposes Proposition 43. “I authored ACA 22 not because I wanted it to become law,” she posted, saying it was the only way to get the other initiative off the ballot in time, the LA Times reported (LA Times, July 6, 2026 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits)). The Orange County Register’s editorial board also noted that Democratic lawmakers who placed it on the ballot are asking voters to reject it (Orange County Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/09/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-43-to-make-it-harder-to-raise-taxes/)).

Court decisions created “loopholes” in Proposition 13, and the measure “restores the two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes.”
Local governments “have imposed over 2,000 new or higher taxes in the past decade.”
Some cities charge real estate transfer taxes “as high as 6%,” which on a $900,000 home would cost a seller $54,000.
It “requires governments to spend tax revenue for the specific purpose voters approved” and “guarantees voters the right to vote on all local taxes.”
The opponents’ rebuttal says the measure “doesn’t cut your taxes a penny” and lets “just 33.4% of voters veto what nearly 67% want.” It was signed by Nick Lapis (Californians Against Waste), Bill Barnes (Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California) and Steve Frisch (Sierra Business Council) (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument against, signed by Darrell Roberts (California Professional Firefighters), Chris Harkins (Nurse Alliance of SEIU California) and Adam Weinberger (California School Employees Association) (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
It lets “just one-third of voters (33.4%) block local voter decisions.”
It “makes it harder to fund fire and police services,” roads, schools and health care.

The cityhallpass page is very informative. Key data points:

**Money raised (Jan 2025 to Nov 1, 2026):**
- For (Yes): $17.56 million (two committees) — largest donor: California Business Roundtable Issues PAC ($11.64M)
- Against (No): $9.20 million — largest donor: SEIU California State Council ($1.5M)

So the Yes side has actually out-raised the No side by ~2:1. Interesting.

**Latest polls:**
- PPIC, Oct 16-22: 42% yes, 55% no
- Berkeley IGS, Oct 19-25: 36% yes, 46% no
- September PPIC: 43% yes, 51% no

’ rebuttal says “the Legislature’s nearly unanimous vote to place Prop. 43 on the ballot” shows courts “exceeded voters’ intent.” It was signed by Jon Coupal (Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association), Michael Hedges (California Small Business Association) and Greg Van Dyke (California Consumer Advocates for Affordability and Safety) (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, head of Reform California, told the Sacramento Bee editorial board he could find savings “to eliminate the need for a tax increase on any ballot in the state of California this cycle” (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/confused-about-how-to-vote-on-proposition-43-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2csuRb)).
Evolve California argues the measure would make California the hardest state in the country to raise local revenue, the Sacramento Bee reported (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/should-local-taxes-require-two-thirds-voter-approval-proposition-43-explained/ar-AA2crlnQ)).
California YIMBY says the measure would make it harder to raise money for “infrastructure upgrades, affordable housing trust funds, and public transportation,” and would push cities toward higher impact fees on new housing (California YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-43-2026/)).
Mott Smith of the Council of Infill Builders, who backed ULA changes, said the industry donors behind the Jarvis initiative “really got absolutely nothing” from the deal (LAist (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/los-angeles-city-mansion-tax-measure-ula-transfer-state-sacramento-ab-736-howard-jarvis-novemeber-ballot-measure)).
Checking the main claims against official records.
Claim Who makes it What official records show
Restores the two-thirds vote for local special taxes Yes campaign (argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)) The text requires two-thirds for new, increased or extended special taxes, including those proposed by initiative, from Jan. 1, 2027 (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). Taxes already approved are not affected (official summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/title-summary.htm)).
Guarantees voters the right to vote on all local taxes Yes campaign The Constitution already requires voter approval of local general taxes (majority) and special taxes (two-thirds) (Art. XIII C, Sec. 2 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C)). Proposition 43 adds no new election requirement for general taxes (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
Requires governments to spend tax money on the purpose voters approved Yes campaign The text contains no spending rule. It sets vote thresholds and the property-tax limit only (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
Protects homeowners from real estate transfer taxes up to 6% Yes campaign The text does not mention transfer taxes. It would require two-thirds for a new or higher transfer tax only if it is a special tax proposed by voters (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop43-text-proposed-laws.pdf)). LA’s ULA rates are 4% and 5.5% (County election results (https://results.lavote.gov/text-results/4300)).
2,000 new or higher local taxes in the past decade Yes campaign We did not find an official count to check this against.
One-third of voters (33.4%) could block a tax No campaign A two-thirds rule means a measure with 66.6% yes fails. The Budget Center gives the example of 35% blocking 65% (California Budget & Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/)).
The Legislature voted nearly unanimously Yes campaign Senate 35-1 and Assembly 68-2, with 13 members not voting. The author and legislative leaders reached the deal to remove another measure (ACA 22 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA22); LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits)).
Makes it harder to fund fire and police No campaign It applies to special taxes proposed by voters. Council-placed special taxes already need two-thirds, and general taxes that can pay for police and fire still need a majority (Art. XIII C, Sec. 2 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C)). The Legislative Analyst says local revenue “could be lower in the future” (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)).
Who supports and opposes it
Supporters
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association of California, California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, California Small Business Association and California Consumer Advocates for Affordability and Safety, which signed the guide arguments (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
California Business Roundtable, through its Issues PAC, the largest donor (Cal-Access, committee 1484860 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484860)).
California Republican Party (CAGOP endorsements (https://cagop.org/endorsements/)).
Reform California and Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (California Budget & Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/); Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/should-local-taxes-require-two-thirds-voter-approval-proposition-43-explained/ar-AA2crlnQ)).
State Senators Shannon Grove, Tony Strickland and Suzette Valladares, whose ballot measure committees paid for slate mailers supporting it (Cal-Access raw data (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
Opponents
California Professional Firefighters, Nurse Alliance of SEIU California, California School Employees Association, California Federation of Teachers, Californians Against Waste, Communities for a Better Environment, AAPI Force, Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California and Sierra Business Council, as listed in the argument against (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
California Democratic Party (Inland Valley News (https://inlandvalleynews.com/california-democratic-party-endorses-2026-general-election-candidates-ballot-measures/); KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-43)).
California State Association of Counties and SEIU California (KQED (https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-43)).
Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, the author (LA Times (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits)), and Evolve California (California Budget & Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/)).
California YIMBY (California YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-43-2026/)).
The League of California Cities’ CITIPAC gave $250,000.01 to the No committee (Cal-Access, committee 1492508 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1492508)). A contribution is not the same as a formal endorsement.
Editorial boards.
Yes: the Southern California News Group, in the Daily News and Orange County Register (Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/08/09/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-43-to-make-it-harder-to-raise-taxes/); Orange County Register (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/08/09/endorsement-yes-on-proposition-43-to-make-it-harder-to-raise-taxes/)), and the San Diego Union-Tribune (San Diego Union-Tribune (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/04/vote-yes-on-prop-43-to-block-state-supreme-courts-rewrite-of-tax-laws/)). The Mercury News and East Bay Times editorial boards also recommend yes, writing that it “merits support” (Mercury News, Oct. 17, 2026 (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/17/endorsement-back-prop-43-restore-voter-approved-restrictions-on-local-taxes-proposition-13/)).
No: the Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/confused-about-how-to-vote-on-proposition-43-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2csuRb)).
Neither: the San Francisco Chronicle editorial board wrote, “We don’t support Prop 43 because it further cements a broken system. But ultimately, we won’t oppose it, either” (San Francisco Chronicle, Oct. 23, 2026 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-43-ballot-california-22477053.php)).
We found no LA Times editorial board position as of Sept. 30, 2026.
Money for and against
For Proposition 43 Against Proposition 43
Committees Two: Yes on Prop 43 - The Local Taxpayer Protection Act (ID 1484860) and Yes on Prop. 43, a Project of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (ID 1493012) One: No on Prop 43: Stop the Local Taxpayer Deception Act, sponsored by labor organizations (ID 1492508)
Raised, Jan. 1, 2025 to Oct. 17, 2026 $15,417,784.02 $7,742,284.74
Spent, same period $15,567,031.80 $6,622,177.15
Cash on hand, Oct. 17, 2026 $244,784.93 $1,152,357.59
Late contributions reported Oct. 18 to Nov. 1 $2,141,383.93 $1,459,000
Source: the committees’ campaign statements for committee 1484860 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484860), committee 1493012 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1493012) and committee 1492508 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1492508), read from the Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip) dated Nov. 2, 2026, and added up by CityHallPass. The latest statements cover Sept. 20 to Oct. 17 (1484860 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3215138&amendid=0); 1493012 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3214623&amendid=0); 1492508 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3215820&amendid=0)). Late contributions are from the committees’ 24-hour reports filed Oct. 19 to Nov. 1, including (1484860: Oct. 19 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3212581&amendid=0), Oct. 20 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3213212&amendid=0), Oct. 21 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3214087&amendid=0), Oct. 22 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3215517&amendid=0), Oct. 22 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3215661&amendid=0); 1493012: Oct. 20 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3213215&amendid=0), Oct. 21 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3213987&amendid=0); 1492508: Oct. 20 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/PDFGen/pdfgen.prg?filingid=3213523&amendid=0)). The No committee reported $32,250 in unpaid bills on Oct. 17. The Secretary of State’s compiled totals (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-43-aca-22-wicks-local-taxes-limitation-res-ch-132-2026) still ran only through Aug. 2 when checked on Sept. 30.
Most of the Yes money was raised before the June 25 deal, when the main committee was working to qualify the Jarvis initiative. Of the $16.68 million in contributions to committee 1484860 through Nov. 1, $2,531,896.67 came in on or after June 25 (Cal-Access, committee 1484860 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484860)). It paid National Political Consultants $12,808,893.92 for petition circulation, 96.5% of its payments. It had $384,461.54 in unpaid bills on Oct. 17 (Cal-Access raw data (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)).
Who is giving
Method: every itemized contribution on the committees’ Form 460 statements from Jan. 1, 2025 to Oct. 17, 2026, plus late contribution reports through Nov. 1, from the Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip). Categories are ours, based on the donor’s name and reported employer.
For: the main Yes committee (ID 1484860).
75 donors gave $16,682,288.53. The California Business Roundtable Issues PAC gave $11,640,000 (69.8%) in 21 payments from Nov. 26, 2025 to Oct. 29, 2026.
Protect Prop. 13, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association’s general committee, gave $1,038,217.78 in mailers and phone calls from January to March 2026. Right Path California Issues PAC gave $584,310.54 in October, $168,724.25 of it in kind.
Real estate owners, developers, managers and brokers gave $2,486,436.13 (14.9%), led by Douglas Emmett Properties ($1,000,000), Kilroy Realty ($1,000,000), McCourt Partners Real Estate ($100,000), Andrew Schwartzberg of Housing Inc. ($100,000) and Moss Management Services ($85,000). That is 62.1% of the money that did not come from the Roundtable or the Jarvis committee.
Other large donors: 1800 Capital, Inc. ($500,000) and Jerry Greenberg, CEO of Sushi Nozawa ($250,000).
98.9% of the money came from donors with California addresses.
Type of donor Donors Amount Share
California Business Roundtable Issues PAC 1 $11,640,000.00 69.8%
Real estate firms and people 41 $2,486,436.13 14.9%
Other businesses, groups and individuals 32 $1,517,634.62 9.1%

Source: Cal-Access, committee 1484860 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1484860), analyzed by CityHallPass. Related entities of one owner are counted separately.
For: the Howard Jarvis Yes committee (ID 1493012). It raised $850,780.55 through Oct. 17. Of that, $475,000 came from Protect Prop. 13, and $580,951.89 was itemized from about 730 donors, most giving $500 or less. It spent $458,804 on radio through Drew Hayes Media and paid $48,490.05 to the association’s spokesperson for campaign work (Cal-Access, committee 1493012 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1493012)).
Against (ID 1492508). 36 donors gave $9,201,284.74 through Oct. 30, all from July 30 on. Unions gave $6,776,747.93 (73.7%). SEIU committees gave $3,598,928.03 (39.1%): the SEIU California State Council ($1,503,928.03), SEIU Local 2015 ($1,000,000), SEIU Local 1021 ($500,000), SEIU Local 721 ($500,000), SEIU Local 99 ($75,000), SEIU Local 121RN ($10,000) and SEIU’s national fund ($10,000). Other donors: California Professional Firefighters ($846,379), the Western States and North Coast regional councils of Carpenters ($500,000 each), the California Teachers Association ($500,000), California Federation of Teachers ($250,000), Operating Engineers Local 3 ($250,000), AFSCME committees ($275,000), the California Alliance for Jobs ($500,000), the Southern California Partnership for Jobs ($500,000), the League of California Cities CITIPAC ($250,000.01), the NPH Action Fund ($202,805.15), the San Francisco Foundation ($300,000), the California Community Foundation ($200,000), the Silicon Valley Community Foundation ($100,000), the ACLU of Northern California ($100,000) and Million More Voters, sponsored by the California Labor Federation ($50,000) (Cal-Access, committee 1492508 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1492508)). The California Community Foundation, which listed a Los Angeles address, also gave $400,000 to the City’s Measure FD campaign (our Measure FD page (https://cityhallpass.com/election-2026/measures/measure-fd)).
Where committee donors get their money. From the committees’ own state filings in the Cal-Access raw data export (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip):
California Business Roundtable Issues PAC (Cal-Access (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1264590)): $14,105,651 in itemized receipts on statements covering Oct. 20, 2024 to Oct. 17, 2026, led by Peter Thiel ($3,000,000), Eric Schmidt ($2,580,301), Kim DeGeorge ($1,930,000), Farmers Group ($1,500,000), Brookfield Property Group ($1,000,000) and Chris Larsen ($750,000). The PAC’s receipts are not earmarked, so these donors did not necessarily pay for Proposition 43.
SEIU California State Council for Working People (Cal-Access (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=960895)): its itemized receipts from Oct. 20, 2024 to Oct. 17, 2026 were $100,385.08, all from the SEIU California State Council itself.
SEIU Local 1021 Issues PAC (Cal-Access (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1296947)): all itemized receipts came from SEIU Local 1021.
League of California Cities CITIPAC (Cal-Access (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1254399)): $547,429.41 in itemized receipts from Oct. 20, 2024 to Oct. 17, 2026, 33.3% from the League itself and the rest from businesses such as waste haulers and utilities.
California Professional Firefighters Ballot Issues Committee (Cal-Access (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=861767)): its only itemized receipt on these statements was $250,000 from the IAFF’s FirePAC.
Outside spending
Committees reported these independent expenditures naming Proposition 43 on Form 496 through Oct. 25 (Cal-Access raw data (https://campaignfinance.cdn.sos.ca.gov/dbwebexport.zip)):
Supporting: Reform California with Carl DeMaio, ballot measure committee, $148,862.20 (door hangers, lawn signs, slate mailers, campaign management); Senator Tony Strickland’s committee, $14,000; Senator Shannon Grove’s committee, $10,500; Senator Suzette Valladares’s committee, $3,000 (the three senators’ committees for slate mailers and voter guides); Republican Party of San Diego County, $2,531.67 (literature).
Opposing: Faith Votes, sponsored by PICO California Action Fund, $38,720.83 (digital ads, phone banking); ACLU California Action Issues Committee, $8,988.70 (voter guide, digital ads); Million Voter Project Action Fund, $5,299.09; ACLU Foundation of San Diego & Imperial Counties, $5,206.21; Justice CA: Isaac Bryan Ballot Measure Committee, $5,000 (slate mailer); Community Partners, $3,915.14; Youth Power PAC, $3,815.66; Council of Community Housing Organizations, $3,120.71; AAPI Equity Alliance, $986.55. Many of these amounts are the filers’ estimates.
Independent analysis
Legislative Analyst. Local tax revenue “could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be.” The effect “is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters” (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/analysis.htm)).
California Budget & Policy Center (a nonprofit that takes no position on measures). It says the rule would reach all special taxes proposed by voters for cities, counties, special districts and school districts, because all taxes of special districts and school districts count as special taxes. It lists ULA among recent majority-approved initiative taxes, with 58% (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/)).
Burke, Williams & Sorensen. The measure “applies prospectively only,” so “local ballot measures approved on or before the November 2026 election are no longer at risk of being invalidated” (California City News (https://www.californiacitynews.org/2026/08/burke-public-law-update-tax-measure-amending-california-constitution-november-ballot.html)).
